key_insight: Stronger LLM reasoning does not guarantee more cooperative behavior: across single-shot social dilemmas, recent models (with or without chain-of-thought) tend to defect. The paper introduces CoopEval, a benchmark to systematically evaluate mechanisms that can sustain cooperation among LLM agents.
problem_solved: Addresses the lack of standardized evaluation for how well LLM agents cooperate in mixed-motive social dilemmas and which interventions actually promote sustained cooperation and safety in multi-agent interactions.
method: Introduce CoopEval: a benchmark suite of social-dilemma environments (e.g., prisoner’s dilemma, public goods) and evaluation protocols (single-shot, repeated, mixed populations).
Empirically evaluate multiple recent LLMs (reasoning enabled/disabled) to measure baseline cooperative tendencies and identify failure modes (consistent defection in single-shot games).

Compare and quantify the effectiveness of cooperation-sustaining mechanisms (e.g., repeated interaction structure, communication/persuasion channels, commitment/trigger strategies, and tailored prompting or incentives) using standardized metrics.
impact: Provides researchers and practitioners a reproducible way to measure and improve cooperation and safety in LLM-driven multi-agent systems, guiding design choices (prompts, training, incentives) for agents that must interact with others in real-world settings.
visual_elements: Heatmap: cooperation rates across LLM models (columns) and game types/settings (rows) highlighting consistent defection in single-shot dilemmas.
Pipeline diagram: CoopEval workflow from environment setup → agent variants → intervention mechanisms → evaluation metrics.
Bar chart: comparative effectiveness of cooperation-sustaining mechanisms (e.g., communication vs. repeated play vs. incentives).
Illustrative icon set: small visuals for key games (Prisoner’s Dilemma, Public Goods), agent dialogue bubble (communication), and a shield (safety/alignment).
paper_title: CoopEval: Benchmarking Cooperation-Sustaining Mechanisms and LLM Agents in Social Dilemmas
paper_authors: Emanuel Tewolde, Xiao Zhang, David Guzman Piedrahita, Vincent Conitzer, Zhijing Jin
